blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The validity of a study is the degree to which its design and conduct support correct conclusions. It has two parts: internal validity (are the conclusions correct for the people studied?) and external validity (do they carry over to other people, places or times?). Before an observed association can be read as an effect, three alternative explanations must be weighed: chance (random variation from studying a sample), bias (a systematic error in how people were selected or measured) and confounding (a mixing of the exposure’s effect with the effect of a third variable).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Recall §11.5, which listed these three and a fourth, reverse causation. Reverse causation is a question of which came first; the design settles it (a cohort measures exposure before outcome, recall §1.5), so this chapter concentrates on the other three.

The three differ in kind. Chance is random: it shrinks as the sample grows, and the confidence interval and p-value measure it (recall §7.2 and §8.5). Bias and confounding are systematic: they push the estimate one way and do not shrink with sample size (recall §6.4). A larger study removes chance and leaves bias and confounding exactly where they were, now with a narrower confidence interval around the wrong answer.

The word “validity” also has two meanings in this book. Instrument validity (recall §16.2) asks whether a tool measures the right construct. Study validity asks whether the whole study supports its conclusion; in this epidemiological sense validity is the absence of systematic error and precision the absence of random error (recall §16.4). A valid instrument used in a badly designed study still gives an invalid result.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A trial of a new oral rehydration regimen (hypothetical figures), run with care in a tertiary hospital, finds fewer treatment failures in the intervention arm, RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.89). The three questions in order: Chance? The interval excludes 1, so chance alone is an unlikely explanation. Bias? Were outcomes assessed by staff who knew the arm, and were children lost from one arm more than the other? Confounding? Randomisation balanced the arms on average. If all three are answered, the result is internally valid for hospitalised children. Whether it holds for children treated at a PHC is the separate question of external validity.

points.html: Ask the questions in order: chance, bias, confounding, then generalisability. A p-value answers only the first.
A statistical technique can be applied with perfect arithmetic to a biased or confounded comparison. Statistical rigour and design rigour are separate requirements.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Internal validity is the degree to which the association observed among the study participants reflects the true effect of the exposure in those participants, with chance, bias and confounding ruled out as far as possible.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Within this study, among these people, is the comparison fair and the measurement true? Each systematic threat in the rest of this chapter is a way internal validity fails: selection bias (§17.2.1), information bias (§17.2.2) and confounding (§17.3).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In an RCT the investigator assigns the exposure at random, which makes the arms alike, on average, in measured and unmeasured characteristics (recall §1.5; §15.9 develops the design). Confounding is then answered by design. An observational cohort or case-control study (recall §1.5) must instead measure the confounders and adjust for them (recall §11.7 and §12.4), and can do nothing about the ones it did not measure (§17.3).

points.html: Internal validity is a precondition for external validity. A result that is wrong for the people studied has nothing correct to generalise, however representative the sample.
Randomisation protects against confounding. It does not protect against bias: an unblinded outcome assessor or unequal loss to follow-up can bias a randomised trial.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: External validity (generalisability) is the degree to which a result that is internally valid for the study participants holds for another target population, setting or time.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: External validity is a question about whether the effect is the same elsewhere, not about whether the sample looks like the population. A sample that differs from the target population in age, severity or setting limits generalisability only if the effect itself differs across those characteristics (effect modification, recall §11.7). This is why a non-representative sample does not by itself make a study invalid: it is a threat to external validity, and it becomes a threat to internal validity only when selection depends on both exposure and outcome (selection bias, §17.2.1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A nutrition trial run in urban, well-resourced hospital patients shows a genuine effect. Rural PHC patients differ in baseline nutrition, access to follow-up and causes of malnutrition. If the intervention works through a mechanism that depends on those features (for example, it corrects a deficiency that is commoner in rural children), the effect may be larger or smaller there. Whether it transfers is a judgement about effect modification, informed by biology and by trials in other settings.

points.html: Strict eligibility criteria and intensive monitoring strengthen internal validity and can narrow the population to which the result applies. This trade-off is a deliberate design choice.

Probability sampling from the target population (recall §6.2) supports generalisation of descriptive estimates such as a prevalence. For an effect estimate, the stronger evidence is consistency across settings.

questions.prompt: A rigorous RCT conducted only at a single urban tertiary hospital shows that a treatment works, with excellent internal validity. A district health officer wants to apply the finding in rural PHCs. What should she consider first, and what kind of evidence would answer it?
questions.answer: External validity: whether the effect is the same in rural PHC patients. That depends on whether the effect is modified by the ways PHC patients differ (severity, baseline nutrition, co-morbidity, adherence, follow-up care). The best evidence is consistency: trials or well-conducted observational studies in similar settings, or subgroup results from the original trial (tested for interaction) for patients like hers. Internal validity was the precondition, and it is met.

questions.prompt: Explain why internal and external validity can pull against each other in study design.
questions.answer: Choices that strengthen internal validity (narrow eligibility, standardised protocols, intensive monitoring, excluding people likely to drop out) make the participants and conditions less like routine practice. The effect is then estimated cleanly but for a narrower population, so its transfer to others rests more on judgement.

questions.prompt: Study A (n = 120) reports RR 1.9 (95% CI 0.9 to 4.0). Study B (n = 12,000), using the same exposure questionnaire with the same systematic error, reports RR 1.35 (95% CI 1.25 to 1.46). Which alternative explanation has Study B’s size dealt with, and which has it not?
questions.answer: Chance: B’s interval is narrow and excludes 1, so random variation is an unlikely explanation for its association. Size does nothing for bias or confounding: the same measurement error is present in B, and the narrow interval is now centred on an estimate that is still biased by it. (Confounding, too, is unchanged by n.)
